title: Road signs and traffic signals
summary: The visual language of the road: sign shapes and colours, markings, signals and hand signals — 255 signs with an identification game.

lessons.title: Shapes, colours and the three sign families
objectives: Classify any Indian road sign as mandatory, cautionary or informatory from its shape and colour.
Know the two signs with unique shapes: Stop and Give way.
Explain why markings and signals belong to the same system.
lessons.intro: India's road signs follow a code of practice from the Indian Roads Congress (IRC:67). The code uses a small set of shapes and colours so you can understand a sign's type from a distance, long before you can read its symbol.

p: Mandatory signs are orders. Breaking one is an offence. A red ring tells you what you must not do: no entry, no overtaking, no U-turn, speed limits, weight limits. A blue circle tells you what you must do: turn left, keep left, compulsory cycle track. Two mandatory signs have their own shapes so they can be recognised even from behind or when covered in dirt: the red octagon STOP and the inverted triangle GIVE WAY.

A triangle with a red border pointing upwards warns of a hazard ahead: a bend, a school, a narrow bridge, a hump, a railway crossing, falling rocks. A warning sign does not order you to do something specific, but it does tell you to slow down and prepare.

Rectangular signs give information: directions, distances, facilities such as fuel, hospitals and parking. On national highways and expressways, direction signs are often green; on other roads, blue or white. Brown is used for tourist destinations.

Road markings are signs painted on the road. A solid centre line means do not cross; a broken line means you may cross when safe. A stop line marks where you must stop at a signal or STOP sign. Traffic signals control the order of movement; a flashing amber means proceed with caution, a flashing red means stop and go only when clear.

note.text: If a sign is hidden by a tree or covered in dust, its shape still tells you whether it is an order, a warning or information.

terms: A sign that gives an order; disobeying it is an offence.
A triangular sign warning of a hazard ahead.
A rectangular sign giving directions or information.
The Indian Roads Congress code of practice for road signs.
examples: A red ring with a number 40 is a mandatory speed limit. A triangle showing a children symbol warns of a school; slow down even if no speed limit is posted.
mistakes: Treating warning triangles as optional because they do not show a rule.
Mixing up GIVE WAY (slow, be ready to stop) with STOP (always stop fully).
safety: Slow down at every warning triangle until you can see the hazard it refers to.

check.q: A circular sign with a red border is:
o: A prohibition — an order not to do something
check.r: Red-ringed circles are mandatory prohibitions. Blue circles are mandatory positive instructions.

check.q: Why do STOP and GIVE WAY have unique shapes?
o: So they can be recognised even from behind or when the face is unreadable
check.r: The octagon and inverted triangle are unmistakable from any angle, which matters at junctions.

check.q: A triangular sign with a red border warns you of:
check.r: Upward-pointing red-bordered triangles are cautionary signs.
